q: Consider the electoral college for the President: 1-Nominated members of Parliament vote. 2-Elected members of Legislative Councils vote. 3-Elected members of the Delhi and Puducherry Assemblies vote. Which is/are correct?
expl: Only Delhi/Puducherry Assemblies vote; nominated members and all Council members are excluded.
why: Council members are excluded whether elected or nominated, which is why the word elected in the second statement is a decoy.
trapnote: No Council member and no nominated member votes. Only elected MPs and elected MLAs do.

q: Consider the electoral college for the Vice-President: 1-Members of both Houses vote. 2-Nominated members vote. 3-Members of State Legislative Assemblies vote. Which is/are correct?
expl: Both Houses including nominated members vote; State legislatures do not.
why: The Vice-Presidential college differs from the Presidential one on both limbs, which is the whole comparison.
trapnote: Nominated members vote for the Vice-President but not for the President. State legislatures vote for neither.

q: A Bill passed by both Houses is returned by the President and re-passed without amendment. Which statement is correct?
options: The President may return it once more for reconsideration
The President may reserve it for the consideration of the Governor
The President may withhold assent if the Bill is a Money Bill
The President must assent, no further option remaining
expl: The return is available once; re-passage obliges assent.
why: The third option inverts the direction of reservation, which runs from Governor to President and never the reverse.
trapnote: Return is available once only. Reservation runs upward from a Governor, never downward.

q: Consider the options open to a Governor on a Bill passed by the State legislature: 1-Assent. 2-Withhold assent. 3-Reserve it for the consideration of the President. Which is/are correct?
expl: All three are available, together with return for reconsideration.
why: The Governor has four options against the President's three, the fourth being reservation.
trapnote: Four options for a Governor, three for the President. Reservation is the difference.

q: On the pardoning powers, which statement is correct?
options: The President may pardon a death sentence; a Governor may not
A Governor may pardon a death sentence; the President may not
Both may pardon a death sentence, the Governor requiring prior consultation
Neither may pardon a death sentence once the sentence is confirmed on appeal
expl: A Governor may commute or remit but cannot pardon a death sentence, nor touch a court martial.
why: The distinction is by type of sentence and by type of court, and both limbs are tested.
trapnote: Two things only the President can reach: a death sentence pardon and a court martial.

q: An ordinance is promulgated while the legislature is not in session. Which statement is correct?
options: It ceases to operate on the date the legislature reassembles
It continues until expressly repealed by the legislature
It ceases to operate six weeks after the reassembly of the legislature
It ceases to operate six months after the date of promulgation
expl: The six-week clock runs from reassembly, not from promulgation.
why: The fourth option runs the clock from the wrong event, which is the commonest error here.
trapnote: The clock starts at reassembly. Nothing turns on the date of promulgation.

q: On repeated re-promulgation of ordinances without laying them: 1-It was held a fraud on the Constitution. 2-The case arose where the practice was systematic. 3-A later decision held failure to lay to be an abuse. Correct?
expl: All three are accurate.
why: The practice involved hundreds of ordinances kept alive for years, which is the fact that fixes the case in memory.
trapnote: Re-promulgation without laying is a fraud on the Constitution. The later decision reinforced it.

q: Consider the 2003 amendment on the Council of Ministers: 1-It capped the Council at fifteen per cent of the House. 2-It prescribed a floor of twelve ministers for States. 3-It barred a disqualified defector from ministerial office. Which is/are correct?
expl: All three limbs belong to the same amendment.
why: The floor for States is the limb most often omitted from summaries of this amendment.
trapnote: Three limbs in one amendment: the cap, the State floor and the bar on defectors.

q: On the removal of the President and of the Vice-President, which statement is correct?
options: The President by impeachment; the Vice-President by an upper House resolution the lower agrees to
Both are removed by impeachment on a charge of violation of the Constitution
The Vice-President is removed by impeachment; the President by a resolution of both Houses
Both are removed by a resolution of the upper House agreed to by the lower House
expl: Impeachment applies to the President alone; the Vice-President is removed by resolution.
why: The Vice-Presidential process specifies no grounds, which is a further point of distinction.
trapnote: Impeachment is for the President alone, and only the Vice-Presidential process specifies no grounds.

q: Consider a Governor's tenure: 1-He holds office during the pleasure of the President. 2-He may be removed by impeachment. 3-His normal term is five years. Which is/are correct?
expl: Pleasure and a five-year term are correct; impeachment does not apply to a Governor.
why: No grounds and no procedure are prescribed for a Governor's removal, which is why impeachment feels plausible.
trapnote: A Governor is recalled at pleasure. No impeachment, no prescribed grounds, no prescribed procedure.

q: A Governor receives a State Bill repugnant to a Union law. Which courses are constitutionally open?
options: Assent, withhold, return once (except Money Bills), or reserve for the President
Only assent or withhold, nothing else
Return it any number of times
Amend the Bill personally and pass it
expl: Four settled courses on a Bill; reservation is the route for repugnancy or constitutional doubt.
why: The textbook four options cover all cases. Repugnancy makes reservation, not rejection, the proper route.
trapnote: Reservation is referral, not rejection.

q: Consider the pardoning power: 1-It is exercised on ministerial advice. 2-It is wholly immune from judicial review. 3-It may be reviewed where the order is mala fide. Which is/are correct?
expl: It is exercised on advice and is reviewable on limited grounds including mala fides.
why: The second and third statements are direct opposites, so one of them must be the planted defect.
trapnote: Limited review applies: mala fides, irrelevant considerations and non-application of mind.

q: A Governor exercises a function in his discretion. Which statement is correct?
options: Discretion is expressly contemplated for a Governor but not for the President
Discretion is expressly contemplated for both the President and a Governor
Discretion is expressly contemplated for the President but not for a Governor
Neither holds discretion, both being bound by ministerial advice in all cases
expl: The State provision expressly contemplates discretion; the Union provision does not.
why: This single structural difference explains most of the litigation about Governors.
trapnote: Discretion is a Governor's feature. The President acts on advice in all cases.

q: On the term and qualifications of the President, which statement is correct?
options: Five years, minimum age thirty, and qualified for election to the lower House
Six years, minimum age thirty-five, and qualified for election to the upper House
Five years, minimum age thirty-five, and qualified for election to the lower House
Five years, minimum age thirty-five, and qualified for election to the upper House
expl: Thirty-five years and qualification for the lower House.
why: The qualification is by reference to the directly elected House, which is the limb most often mistaken.
trapnote: Age thirty-five and lower-House qualification. A Governor mirrors this with Assembly qualification.

q: Consider the office of Vice-President: 1-He is ex officio Chairman of the upper House. 2-He is a member of that House. 3-He acts as President when that office falls vacant. Which is/are correct?
expl: He chairs the House without being a member, and acts as President on a vacancy.
why: Not being a member is the point most often missed, and it explains why he has no ordinary vote.
trapnote: He presides without membership. That is why he has a casting vote only.

q: When the office of Vice-President falls vacant, which statement is correct?
options: The President appoints an acting Vice-President until an election is held
The Deputy Chairman performs the Chairman's duties; there is no acting Vice-President
The Chief Justice discharges the functions of the Vice-President
The Speaker of the lower House discharges those functions
expl: There is no office of acting Vice-President; the Deputy Chairman presides.
why: The confusion arises because the Vice-President does act as President on a vacancy in that office.
trapnote: One office has an acting arrangement, the other does not. Keep the two vacancies distinct.

q: A person acts as President on a vacancy in that office. For what maximum period may this continue?
expl: The vacancy must be filled within six months.
why: All four options are periods used elsewhere in the Constitution, which is what makes them plausible.
trapnote: Six months is the outer limit. The other periods in the options belong to other provisions.

q: Consider the veto powers of the President: 1-Absolute veto. 2-Suspensive veto. 3-Pocket veto. Which is/are available in practice?
expl: All three are available, the pocket veto arising because no time limit is prescribed.
why: The pocket veto is not a named power; it exists because the provision fixes no period for action.
trapnote: The pocket veto is a consequence of silence in the text, not an express power.

q: On an ordinance promulgated by a Governor, which statement is correct?
options: Prior instructions from the President are needed in every case
No instructions are needed, the power being co-extensive with the President's
Instructions are needed only where the legislature is bicameral
Prior instructions from the President are needed in specified cases
expl: Specified categories require prior instructions; the power is otherwise independent.
why: The second option overstates a real requirement into a universal one, which is the usual construction.
trapnote: A real requirement confined to specified cases is often presented as universal.

q: Consider a Bill reserved by a Governor for the President: 1-The President may assent or withhold assent. 2-The President may direct the Governor to return it. 3-If the House re-passes it, the President must assent. Which is/are correct?
expl: The President is not obliged to assent even after re-passage of a reserved Bill.
why: This is where the reserved route differs sharply from the ordinary Union route, and the difference is the point.
trapnote: Re-passage compels assent at the Union level but not on a Bill reserved by a Governor.
